Testimony ofRepresentative Dan Shagoury introducing
LD 1148, An Act to Improve Access to Absentee Ballots for Municipal

Elections for Uniformed Service Voters and Overseas Voters

Before the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee

Good morning Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs. I am Representative Dan Shagoury, and I represent
House District 55 - the communities of Hallowell, Manchester and West Gardiner. I come before
you today to introduce LD 1148, An Act to Improve Access to Absentee Ballots for
Municipal Elections for Uniformed Service Voters and Overseas Voters.

A constituent came to me with a problem. Her daughter, Kate, was studying in England and
wanted to vote in the state and local elections in Hallowell, Maine. Kate requested a ballot from the Secretary of State's Office, and received only the state ballot. She was surprised that all she got was the state ballot -- she wasn't informed that you have to request municipal and local
school district ballots directly from your home community. Apparently this is a fairly common
occurrence, and as a result a fair number of people overseas miss out on voting in their local
elections.

Kate was able to work things out with the City Clerk in Hallowell to get her a local absentee
ballot in time, but this prompted her and her family to ask me if we could come up with a better, simpler way that would help ensure overseas and uniformed voters can vote in municipal and local school district elections. After some discussions with the Secretary of State's Office, we
came up with the idea in this bill.
This bill directs municipalities to send a copy of their local ballots to the state, then when the
overseas voter requests a ballot from the Secretary of State's office they are sent both the state
and local ballots. This is not only easier for the overseas voter, who only has to send one request, it is also easier for the municipal clerks, who only have to send one ballot to the Secretary of
State. This saves them the time and expense of processing lots of ballot requests from overseas
voters.

Of course this will only work when local elections coincide with state-wide elections, but when they line up it will be a much more convenient process for both the overseas voter and the
municipal clerks.
Thank you for your consideration. I look forward to working with you on this bill. You will be
hearing from the Secretary of State's Office after me, and they can provide you with more detailed answers, but I will be glad to attempt to answer any questions.

Dear Senator Hickman, Rep. Supica and Members of the Committee:
My name is Kristin Aiello. I am a resident of Hallowell where I am an attorney in private
practice. I have been lead counsel in seminal voting rights cases including Doe, er al v. Rowe, el al, 156 2d 35 (D. Me. 2001), cited in Tennessee v. Lane, 541 U.S. 509 (2004) and Merrill, et al v. Dunlap, el al, l:20-cv-00248-JAW (2020) (creating an accessible absentee ballot system for
individuals who are blind or visually impaired or with other print disabilities). In addition to casework, I have made presentations to the legal community in both local and national seminars
on voting rights.
I am here to express my strong support for LD l 148, An Act to Improve Access to Absentee
Ballols for Municipal Elections for Uniformed Service Members and Overseas Voters. This critical piece of legislation seeks to ensure that uniformed service members and overseas voters are able to participate in municipal and school elections by allowing them to vote via absentee ballots, in line with the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA).
The issue of municipal absentee ballots not being provided to overseas voters most recently
came to my attention in October, 2023. My daughter, Kate, a Hallowell resident, was (and currently
is) living overseas as a graduate student. In 2023, Kate wanted to vote in the November 7 elections
back home, and so on October 8, 2023, she requested an electronic UOCAVA Ballot by using the
State of Maine Absentee Ballot Request Service for uniformed and overseas citizens.` On October
l2, 2023, the Secretary of State's Office processed and approved Kate's application, noting that
she is a registered voter in Hallowell and providing instructions on how to access her secure ballot
online. Kate followed the instructions, voted on the state ballot provided to her, and returned her ballot electronically. But a ballot for the municipal election in Hallowell was not included in the ballots electronically sent to her so she was not able to vote at that time in her local election.
` In contrast to UOCAVA voters, the Absentee Ballot Request page for the Secretary of State instructs Maine voters
currently living in the U.S. to contact their municipal clerk.
vwvw.aietloIawmaine.com

Because Kate noticed that she was not provided with an absentee ballot for the municipal election that she knew was being held, she requested one from Hallowell, but it was unclear if her ballot would be returned by Election Day via the mail. Coincidentally, a family member was going abroad to visit her at this time and was able to hand deliver the ballot to her and back to Hallowell in time to be counted. But this experience highlighted a systemic and serious flaw in the system
that needs to be addressed: Uniformed service members and overseas citizens (UOCAVA voters)
who request absentee ballots online are not provided with municipal and local ballots. Therefore,
they are commonly, if not always. denied their right to vote in local elections. This is unacceptable.
Uniformed service members and overseas voters are vital to our democracy, often serving in regions far from home and facing unique challenges when it comes to voting. Unfortunately,
under the current system, most, if not all, of these voters are effectively disenfranchised in local
elections. UOCAVA allows service members and overseas citizens to vote in federal and state
elections, but it currently does not extend to local elections, including crucial votes on school budgets, local governance, and municipal decisions.
This gap in access is a significant issue. UOCAVA voters, who are living or stationed in
different parts ofthe world, do not receive ballots for local elections, depriving them of their right to have a voice in decisions that directly impact their communities. Municipal elections, including those concerning school budgets and local government, are fundamental to the quality of life for
those who continue to serve our country and represent us abroad. These elections decide everything
from funding for local schools to vital community services that often have a profound impact on both their hometowns and their families back home.
Without the ability to cast their ballots in these local elections, uniformed service members and overseas citizens face a substantial loss of their rights as American citizens. As it stands, they are often excluded from determining local leadership and important community decisions, a
situation that is, again, simply unacceptable.
By passing LD 1148, we are improving access and better ensuring that our service
members, who are already sacrificing so much, are not further excluded from the democratic process at the local level. It is essential that we honor their service by providing them the means
to participate in all elections, including those that affect their hometowns and their families.
Allowing these voters to cast their ballots online or through other secure absentee voting
methods for local and school elections will empower them to exercise their right to vote and ensure their voices are heard in decisions that affect them directly. This is a matter of fairness, equality, and respect for those who serve our country.
As aptly held by the United States Supreme Court,
Undoubtedly, the right of suffrage is a fundamental matter in a free and democratic society. Especially since the right to exercise the franchise in a free and unimpaired manner is preservative of other basic civil and political rights, any alleged infringement of the right of citizens to vote must be carefully and meticulously scrutinized.

Reynolds v. Sims, 377, U.S. 533, 561-62 (1964).
l urge you to support LD l 148 and help ensure that all Maine voters--regardless of where
they are stationed or temporarily reside--have equal access to participate in the full spectrum of elections that shape their communities, because, "for reasons too self-evident to warrant amplification. . .voting is of the most fundamental significance under our constitutional structure." Ill. State Board of Elections v. Socialist Workers Party, 440 U.S. 174, 184 (I979).
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Uniformed Service and Overseas Voters

Position:

SUPPORT

The Maine Town & City Clerks' Association is in support of LD 1148 and we thank you for the opportunity to outline our points for your committee.

Members were in favor of having the Secretary of State issue ballots electronically to UOCAVA voters in municipal elections but questioned whether the service would be available when the municipal election is not held on the same day as a state election. Inconsistency with election procedures is difficult for voters to understand.

The language in Section 6 of the bill was unclear regarding whether "a copy of the local ballot" required to be provided was a paper ballot or an electronic copy.

Clerks wondered what the timeline would be to provide the ballot to the state in order to be included in the electronic ballot process, since each municipality has different timelines for finalizing their slate of candidates.

Members felt that providing municipal ballots with state ballots to UOCAVA voters may increase the return rate of those absentee ballots for local elections. Members did express concern on how the voted ballots would be returned to municipalities to be counted on election night.

The Maine Town & City Clerks' Association appreciates the opportunity to share its testimony with the Committee. Should any questions arise, please feel free to contact me at (207)680-4210 or by email: pdubois@waterville-me.gov .

Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
Neither For Nor Against LD 1148 - An Act to Improve Access to Absentee Ballots for Municipal Elections for Uniformed Service
Voters and Overseas Voters March 31, 2025
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, my name is Rebecca Lambert, and I am providing testimony in opposition to LD 1148 on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's (MMA) elected 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). For reference, MMA is a nonpartisan, nonprofit member service organization and aims to help provide policy solutions that work for all residents in Maine and the LPC guides the advocacy efforts and establishes positions on bills of municipal interest.
Municipalities across Maine have a vested interest in ensuring that the voting process is accessible, efficient, and fair for all eligible voters, including those working or residing overseas. Likewise, local leaders recognize there are complexities and potential challenges that may arise from this change in procedure.
In general, municipalities fully support the fundamental right of U.S. citizens who are abroad to participate in elections, including those related to local ballot measures and municipal elections. Overseas voters contribute to the diversity and richness of our democratic process, and it is important to ensure that they can vote, just as any other citizen is able to do so. Enabling these voters to have access to local ballots is a meaningful way to extend that right.
Many municipalities have established processes for managing absentee voting and local ballot distribution, and this change could require substantial adjustments to those systems. Although local officials appreciate the intent behind LD 1148, in reality, they fear it could create a logistical nightmare and further question whether the change would improve the process and if the cost would be worthwhile.
Thank you for your time and for considering the municipal perspective on this issue.

Testifying in favor of
L.D. 1148 "An Act to Improve Access to Absentee Ballots for Municipal Elections for Uniformed
Service Voters and Overseas Voters"

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans
and Legal Affairs, my name is Shemia Bellows, I live in Manchester, and I am the Secretary of State. I
am testifying in favor of L.D. 1148 because the policy goal is one the State of Maine should aspire to.
Currently when uniformed service and overseas voters (commonly referred to as UOCAVA voters,
from the Uniformed And Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act) request an absentee ballot, they
receive the appropriate state ballots from the Division of Elections. State ballots for UOCAVA voters
are sent to voters centrally from the Division of Elections, where they are also returned, processed and
counted. UOCAVA voters include active-duty military and their dependents (U.S. Army, Navy, Air
Force and Marine Corps); Coast Guard; commissioned corps of the U.S. Public Health Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration; the Merchant Marine; and any U.S. citizen living
outside of the United States who was qualified or would be qualified to vote in their place of residence
in Maine prior to leaving the United States.
Last November, about 6,600 UOCAVA voters participated in the General Election. As with any other voter, we see greater UOCAVA interest in presidential elections than other types of elections.
This bill would expand the program to allow for electronic return of the municipal ballot through a
system similar to the one the state utilizes for all municipalities. We applaud the policy and note that
there will be substantial implementation challenges that will require significant resources in order to implement with the proper safeguards to protect security and accessibility of our elections.

There is not currently a mechanism by which the Division of Elections can issue local ballots, as local elections are not overseen by the Department of the Secretary of State. This was raised as an issue recently when a Mainer studying abroad requested their ballot and was surprised not to receive their local ballot. It took some work, and the voter received their local ballot, but the issue had clearly been
raised.
101 State House Station, Augusta, Maine 04333-010] www.Maine. gov/sos/cec; tel. 207-624-773 6

This issue is what L.D. 1148 seeks to address. Because each municipality having to procure separately the technology to issue local ballots timely and securely at the municipal level would create significant administrative and financial burdens on the municipalities, L.D. l 148 would have the Division of Elections issue a voter's local ballot for any municipal election for which the uniformed service voter or overseas voter is eligible that is to be held on the same date as a statewide election.
This would require three major investments to modernize our elections to ensure that we continue to
have free, safe and secure elections at every level including 1.) technology; 2.) staffing and 3.)
procedures.
Technology: The Division of Elections would be required to procure a new system that would
accommodate not only state and federal elections but also all of the myriad municipal elections
including school budget and school board elections. We have reached out to our current vendor to
inquire as to a rough estimate of the cost but acknowledge that this would require a new Request for
Proposal (RFP) process in accordance with state procurement rules and could be very costly.
Staffing: The Division of Elections anticipates that this would create significant additional staffing needs at the Division of Elections to train and coordinate timely ballot transmittal from the municipalities into the system. This would expand the current duties of the Division of Elections into municipal election oversight, as we would need to work with potentially up to 500 municipalities on
proper ballot design and timely ballot submission. We anticipate that should the state take this on,
many municipalities would likely change their election dates to coincide with state and federal elections. The Division of Elections is already working overtime in advance of state and federal elections, so we would propose creation of a new section to handle Municipal and Local Services to
ensure that everything is performed legally, accurately, efficiently and securely.
Procedures: The Division of Elections would need to work closely with municipalities on proper procedures for ballot layout and transmittal because of course this proposal would necessitate the
Division of Elections receiving these local ballots in time to issue to the UOCAVA voters (federal requirements are that UOCAVA ballots be issued 45 days prior to the election, for applications filed
ahead of that date). Once any local ballots are voted and returned to the Division of Elections, they would be delivered to the municipality for counting. That too would require proper procedures and
staffing.
We believe this is an important undertaking, though we acknowledge that it is no small task. Should
the committee decide to move forward with this initiative, we stand ready to make it work with the
proper resources.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide this information, and I am happy to answer any questions you may have.
